stances.claim: Nixon's resignation -- rather than cripple the Senate and the nation with a tedious trial -- was the more dignified and ultimately redemptive choice, converting intended humiliation into a personal triumph.

The decisive factor in impeachment is not legal guilt but the people's trust: Clinton was retained because his sexual dalliance did not diminish his ability to run the country; Nixon was forced out because his Watergate lies betrayed his fitness for office.

notable_anecdotes: Nixon's one-sentence resignation letter of August 9, 1974: 'I hereby resign as President of the United States' -- the most economical exit from the most powerful office in the world.
Conrad Black's observation that Nixon 'converted to a personal triumph what was intended to be an unprecedented humiliation.'
Nixon's rehabilitation: after personal anguish, he met Gorbachev in 1986 and ranked in a Gallup poll among the 10 most admired men; at his death in 1994 at 81, five kilometers of mourners lined up.
The Ford pardon: Nixon initially reluctant to accept it (accepting implies guilt) but ultimately did, saying 'No words can describe the depth of my regret and pain.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban uses Nixon's 1974 resignation as the paradigm of choosing dignity over an impeachment trial, then draws the Clinton contrast to identify public trust as the decisive variable. When it became clear that only 15 of 100 senators backed him -- far below the 34 needed to avoid ouster -- Nixon did not filibuster or challenge the proceedings in the US Supreme Court. He submitted his one-sentence resignation letter ('I hereby resign as President of the United States') on August 9, 1974, followed by a live-TV Oval Office valedictory. President Ford's September 8, 1974 pardon was initially resisted but finally accepted; Nixon apologized 'no words can describe the depth of my regret.' Biographer Conrad Black observed he 'converted to a personal triumph what was intended to be an unprecedented humiliation.' After years of anguish, Nixon rehabilitated himself as an elder statesman; his 1994 death drew 50,000 mourners across a five-kilometer line. The Clinton-Nixon contrast is instructive: Clinton was retained because the people did not believe his sexual dalliance impaired his fitness to govern; Nixon was forced out because his repeated Watergate lies betrayed his fitness for office. The decisive factor is always the people's trust -- more political than legal.
